title: Pulmonary Vascular Disease
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers disorders of the pulmonary circulation: fluid leaking into the lung (pulmonary edema), material lodging in the pulmonary arteries (thrombotic, fat, air, and amniotic fluid emboli), death of lung tissue after embolism (pulmonary infarction), sustained high pressure in the pulmonary circuit (pulmonary hypertension), and abnormal arteriovenous connections that bypass the alveoli. Board questions usually give a setting and a blood gas, a wedge pressure, or an autopsy finding and ask you to name the mechanism. If you can apply Starling forces, explain why embolism causes hypoxemia with a low PaCO2, and reason from the dual blood supply and the right ventricle's tolerance of afterload, you can work through most items.
prerequisites: Starling forces and lymphatic drainage of the interstitium
Pulmonary and bronchial circulations and hypoxic vasoconstriction (PU-5)
Ventilation-perfusion matching, dead space, shunt, and the A-a gradient (PU-7)
Coagulation cascade, fibrinolysis, and Virchow triad (hematology)
Right and left ventricular function and the Frank-Starling relationship (cardiovascular)

connections.how: The low-pressure, high-compliance pulmonary bed and its dual supply explain why the right ventricle fails under sudden afterload and why most emboli do not infarct.
ARDS is the prototype of noncardiogenic edema from diffuse alveolar capillary injury.
Left heart failure raises pulmonary venous pressure, causing cardiogenic edema, group 2 pulmonary hypertension, and the poor bronchial flow that permits infarction.
Inherited and acquired hypercoagulable states, D-dimer, and DIC link pulmonary embolism and amniotic fluid embolism to the coagulation system.
Right-to-left shunts through a patent foramen ovale or a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation let venous clots and bacteria reach the brain.

Alveolar macrophages filled with hemosiderin from phagocytosed red cells, a sign of chronic pulmonary venous congestion.
The three conditions that favor thrombosis: venous stasis or turbulent flow, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.
Ventilated lung that receives no perfusion, so it takes no part in gas exchange (ventilation-perfusion ratio of infinity).
The difference between calculated alveolar PO2 and measured arterial PO2; it widens with V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion limitation.
A degradation product of cross-linked fibrin released when plasmin breaks down a clot; sensitive for thrombosis but not specific.
A large thromboembolus lodged across the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery.
Passage of a venous embolus into the systemic arteries through a right-to-left shunt.
Right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, or failure caused by pulmonary hypertension from disease of the lung or its vessels.
A tuft of small, slit-like vascular channels within a dilated segment of a small pulmonary artery, typical of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Blood that passes from the venous to the arterial side without meeting alveolar gas, causing hypoxemia that 100% oxygen corrects poorly.

sections.title: Pulmonary edema: Starling forces, cardiogenic and noncardiogenic

blocks.text: Fluid movement across any capillary follows the Starling relationship: filtration is proportional to the filtration coefficient times the hydrostatic gradient (capillary minus interstitial pressure) minus the reflection coefficient times the oncotic gradient (plasma minus interstitial oncotic pressure). In the lung, capillary hydrostatic pressure is low, about 7 to 10 mmHg, and interstitial pressure is slightly negative, while plasma oncotic pressure is about 25 to 28 mmHg. The result is a small continuous outward leak that lymphatics return to the circulation, so alveoli stay dry.

Three safety factors protect the lung: a large gap between capillary and plasma oncotic pressure, lymph flow that can rise several fold, and washout of interstitial protein as filtration rises, which lowers interstitial oncotic pressure. Edema appears only when these are overwhelmed. Fluid collects first in the loose interstitium around bronchioles and vessels, then breaks through into the alveoli. Interstitial fluid stiffens the lung and stimulates juxtacapillary (J) receptors, causing rapid shallow breathing and dyspnea; alveolar fluid adds crackles, frothy sputum, and hypoxemia from low V/Q units and shunt.

Cardiogenic (hydrostatic) edema follows a rise in left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure from left ventricular failure, mitral stenosis, or volume overload. The wedge pressure is above 18 mmHg and the fluid is a low-protein transudate because the capillary wall is intact. Lying flat returns blood from the legs to the central circulation and raises pulmonary capillary pressure further, which explains orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Red cells leak into alveoli from engorged capillaries, and macrophages convert their hemoglobin iron into hemosiderin, producing heart failure cells; long-standing congestion with fibrosis gives brown induration of the lung.

blocks.title: From left heart failure to alveolar flooding
steps: Left ventricle fails or mitral valve narrows
Left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure rise
Capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds plasma oncotic pressure

Fluid breaks into alveoli; low V/Q and shunt
Dyspnea, crackles, hypoxemia; wedge above 18 mmHg
blocks.caption: Wedge pressure estimates left atrial pressure, so it identifies the hydrostatic cause.

blocks.text: Noncardiogenic edema occurs with a normal wedge pressure (18 mmHg or less). Injury to the alveolar capillary endothelium or epithelium raises permeability and lowers the reflection coefficient, so protein-rich fluid floods alveoli even at normal pressure; this is acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS, PU-14-A). Low plasma oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition) narrows the safety margin, so modest pressure increases cause edema. Lymphatic obstruction, classically tumor spreading through lymphatics (lymphangitic carcinomatosis), removes the drainage that normally keeps pace with filtration.

blocks.title: Cardiogenic versus noncardiogenic edema
rows: Permeability up, oncotic pressure down, or lymph flow down
Left ventricular failure, mitral stenosis, volume overload
ARDS (sepsis, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis), nephrotic syndrome, lymphangitic tumor
Heart failure cells, cardiomegaly, high BNP
Hyaline membranes in ARDS; normal heart size
blocks.caption: Wedge pressure separates the groups; fluid protein reflects whether the capillary wall is intact.

blocks.title: Applying Starling forces to the lung
blocks.text: Using approximate textbook values, outward forces are capillary pressure 7 mmHg, interstitial pressure of -8 mmHg (which pulls fluid outward, adding 8), and interstitial oncotic pressure 14 mmHg, totaling 29 mmHg. The inward force is plasma oncotic pressure, 28 mmHg. Net filtration pressure is about +1 mmHg, which lymphatics easily remove. If left atrial pressure rises so that capillary pressure reaches 30 mmHg, outward force becomes about 52 mmHg and net pressure about +24 mmHg, beyond lymphatic capacity, so edema forms. Acutely, capillary pressure must exceed roughly the plasma oncotic pressure before edema appears; if plasma oncotic pressure is halved, edema appears at a much lower capillary pressure.

About 95% of pulmonary emboli arise from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the legs, mostly from the proximal deep veins (popliteal, femoral, and iliac); calf thrombi embolize less often unless they extend upward. The thrombus breaks free, passes through the right heart, and lodges in a pulmonary artery sized to its diameter. Venous thrombosis follows Virchow triad: stasis (immobility, surgery, long travel, heart failure), endothelial injury (trauma, surgery, prior thrombosis), and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, estrogen-containing contraceptives, factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antiphospholipid antibodies).

Most emboli are small and clinically silent. A significant embolus stops perfusion to ventilated alveoli, creating dead space. Blood is diverted to the remaining lung, where overperfusion creates low V/Q units; platelet mediators (serotonin, thromboxane A2) cause local vasoconstriction and bronchoconstriction, surfactant loss over the next day causes atelectasis, and falling cardiac output lowers mixed venous PO2. Together these widen the A-a gradient and cause hypoxemia. Hypoxemia and stimulation of J and irritant receptors drive hyperventilation; because CO2 is easy to eliminate through the remaining lung, PaCO2 falls and the blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis. A normal or rising PaCO2 suggests massive embolism or fatigue.

blocks.title: From embolus to right heart strain
steps: Leg DVT fragment lodges in pulmonary arteries
Obstruction plus serotonin and thromboxane vasoconstriction
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises abruptly
Thin right ventricle dilates; septum bows left
Left ventricular filling and cardiac output fall
Hypotension, RV ischemia, possible sudden death
blocks.caption: Acute cor pulmonale: the right ventricle cannot hypertrophy in minutes, so it dilates and fails.

blocks.text: The right ventricle normally works against a low-resistance bed and cannot generate a high pressure acutely. When about 60% or more of the bed is obstructed, as with a saddle embolus across the main pulmonary artery bifurcation, the right ventricle dilates, the septum shifts into the left ventricle, and left ventricular filling falls (ventricular interdependence). Right ventricular wall tension rises while systemic pressure, and with it right coronary perfusion, falls, so the ventricle becomes ischemic. Death can occur within minutes, often as pulseless electrical activity.

blocks.title: Findings in pulmonary embolism and their mechanisms
rows: Hypoxemia and J receptor and irritant receptor stimulation
Peripheral infarction or hemorrhage irritating the parietal pleura
Sympathetic response to hypoxemia and falling stroke volume
Low V/Q units, atelectasis, low mixed venous PO2
Plasmin degrading cross-linked fibrin; also high in surgery, cancer, pregnancy
Right heart strain: raised JVP, loud P2, sinus tachycardia, right axis, RBBB, T inversion V1 to V4, raised troponin and BNP
Acute pressure overload and RV ischemia
blocks.caption: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so a normal value argues against embolism when suspicion is low.

blocks.title: The blood gas in pulmonary embolism
blocks.text: A patient breathing room air at sea level has PaO2 65 mmHg and PaCO2 28 mmHg. Alveolar PO2 equals FiO2 times (760 minus 47) minus PaCO2 divided by 0.8: 0.21 times 713 is about 150, and 28 divided by 0.8 is 35, so PAO2 is about 115 mmHg. The A-a gradient is 115 minus 65, about 50 mmHg, far above the normal of about 5 to 15 mmHg in a young adult. Hypoventilation would give a high PaCO2 and a normal gradient; here the low PaCO2 shows hyperventilation, and the wide gradient shows that oxygen transfer itself is impaired by V/Q mismatch.

blocks.predict: An embolus creates dead space, which by itself should raise PaCO2. Why is PaCO2 usually low in pulmonary embolism?
blocks.explain: Hypoxemia and lung receptor stimulation increase minute ventilation far beyond what is needed to clear the extra dead space. CO2 diffuses easily and the CO2 dissociation curve is nearly linear, so overventilated units lower PaCO2, while they cannot add much O2 to blood leaving low V/Q units.

sections.title: Fat, air, and amniotic fluid embolism

blocks.text: Nonthrombotic emboli are recognized by their setting and by the extra injury each material causes beyond simple obstruction. They differ from thromboembolism in timing, in the organs involved, and in the blood findings.

Fat embolism follows fractures of long bones (especially the femur) or the pelvis, and less often orthopedic surgery, liposuction, or extensive burns. Marrow fat globules enter torn marrow veins; they are found in the lungs of most patients with severe skeletal injury, but the fat embolism syndrome develops in only a small minority. Symptoms begin about 24 to 72 hours after injury because the damage is partly biochemical: lipase releases free fatty acids from the globules, and these injure endothelium in the lung and brain, while platelets and neutrophils adhere to the fat. The result is respiratory insufficiency with hypoxemia, neurologic changes (confusion, irritability, delirium, coma), anemia, thrombocytopenia, and a petechial rash over the upper trunk, axillae, and conjunctivae. Deformable globules squeeze through pulmonary capillaries, or through a patent foramen ovale, to reach the brain and skin. Fat in vessels is shown with fat stains such as oil red O on frozen sections.

Air embolism requires more than about 100 mL of air to cause clinical effects. Venous air enters during insertion, disconnection, or removal of a central venous catheter, especially with the patient upright and venous pressure low, or during neck, chest, and obstetric procedures. Air collects as froth in the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries and blocks outflow. Decompression sickness is a special case: under high pressure, more nitrogen dissolves in blood and tissue (Henry law), and when a diver ascends too fast, it comes out of solution as bubbles. These cause joint and muscle pain (the bends), dyspnea and chest pain with pulmonary edema and hemorrhage (the chokes), and neurologic deficits; repeated exposure causes ischemic necrosis of bone, typically the femoral and humeral heads. Bubbles crossing a right-to-left shunt become arterial emboli and cause stroke.

Amniotic fluid embolism is rare but has a high mortality. During labor or just after delivery, amniotic fluid enters the maternal circulation through tears in the uterine veins or placental membranes. Fetal squamous cells, lanugo hair, vernix fat, and mucin lodge in maternal pulmonary vessels, and the fluid triggers an anaphylactoid reaction with complement activation and intense pulmonary vasoconstriction, causing acute right heart failure, then left ventricular dysfunction and diffuse alveolar damage. Its tissue factor activates coagulation and causes disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The mother develops sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, hypotensive shock, and seizures, followed by bleeding. At autopsy, squamous cells in maternal pulmonary arterioles confirm the diagnosis.

blocks.caption: Setting and timing identify the embolus; the extra mechanism explains the findings beyond obstruction.

blocks.text: Only about 10% of pulmonary emboli cause infarction because lung tissue has a dual blood supply. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange, while the bronchial arteries, arising from the thoracic aorta or an upper intercostal artery, nourish the airways, vessels, and connective tissue at systemic pressure. Alveoli also receive oxygen directly from inspired air. When a pulmonary artery branch is blocked, bronchial blood flows through anastomoses into the territory and keeps it alive, often with hemorrhage into alveoli but no necrosis.

Infarction occurs when an embolus blocks a medium or small peripheral artery and the bronchial circulation cannot compensate. The classic setting is left heart failure, in which low cardiac output reduces bronchial inflow and high pulmonary venous pressure impedes drainage; shock, chronic lung disease, and older age add risk. Large central emboli tend to cause right heart strain or sudden death rather than infarction, because the patient dies before necrosis develops or the distal tissue still receives bronchial flow.

blocks.title: Why an embolus infarcts the lung
steps: Embolus blocks a medium or small peripheral artery
Bronchial flow is poor, as in left heart failure
Distal tissue becomes ischemic and dies
Bronchial blood leaks into the dead alveoli
Wedge-shaped red infarct based on the pleura
Fibrinous pleuritis and alveolar hemorrhage
blocks.caption: Dual supply prevents infarction until bronchial flow fails.

blocks.text: About three quarters of infarcts affect the lower lobes, which receive the most blood flow, and they are often multiple. Each is wedge shaped because the occluded artery's territory fans out from the hilum toward the periphery, so the base lies on the pleural surface and the apex points to the hilum. The infarct is hemorrhagic (red) because the loose, spongy lung lets bronchial blood pour into the dead tissue, unlike the pale infarcts of solid organs with a single end-arterial supply such as the heart, kidney, and spleen. Over about 48 hours the red cells lyse, the infarct turns red brown as hemosiderin forms, and it is eventually replaced by a contracted fibrous scar. An infected embolus produces a septic infarct that can form an abscess.

The clinical features follow the anatomy. The visceral pleura lacks pain fibers, but the parietal pleura is innervated by the intercostal and phrenic nerves, so fibrinous exudate over a pleural-based infarct causes sharp pain on breathing and a pleural friction rub. Blood in the alveoli is coughed up as hemoptysis, and a small, often bloody, exudative pleural effusion and low-grade fever may follow. Imaging may show a pleural-based wedge-shaped opacity.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with left heart failure develop a red, wedge-shaped infarct after a small embolus, when a healthy young adult with the same embolus does not?
blocks.explain: In the healthy lung, bronchial arteries perfuse the blocked territory, so tissue survives with at most hemorrhage. In heart failure, low output and high venous pressure reduce bronchial flow, so the tissue dies, while the remaining bronchial blood still leaks into the necrotic, spongy tissue and makes it hemorrhagic.
blocks.check: The dual supply paragraph and the infarction flow.

blocks.text: The normal pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, low-resistance bed (mean pulmonary artery pressure about 15 mmHg) whose thin, compliant vessels recruit and distend as flow rises. Pulmonary hypertension is a resting mean pulmonary artery pressure above about 20 mmHg (25 mmHg in older sources). Pressure equals flow times resistance plus left atrial pressure, so it rises when resistance increases (narrowed, obliterated, or constricted vessels) or when left atrial pressure is transmitted backward. A normal wedge pressure (15 mmHg or less) indicates a precapillary cause; a raised wedge pressure indicates a postcapillary cause from the left heart.

blocks.title: Clinical classification of pulmonary hypertension
rows: Proliferative remodeling of small pulmonary arteries
Idiopathic; heritable (BMPR2); drugs (anorectic agents, methamphetamine); systemic sclerosis; HIV; portal hypertension; left-to-right shunts
Raised left atrial pressure transmitted backward
Left ventricular failure, mitral stenosis or regurgitation (most common cause overall)
Hypoxic vasoconstriction and loss of vascular bed
COPD, interstitial lung disease, sleep apnea, high altitude
Sarcoidosis, myeloproliferative and some metabolic disorders
blocks.caption: Groups 1, 3, and 4 are precapillary; group 2 is postcapillary.

blocks.text: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a disease of the vessel wall itself. Endothelial dysfunction shifts the balance away from vasodilators and antiproliferative mediators (nitric oxide, prostacyclin) toward vasoconstrictors and mitogens (endothelin-1, thromboxane A2). BMPR2 encodes a receptor of the TGF-beta superfamily that normally signals through SMAD proteins to restrain smooth muscle proliferation and promote apoptosis. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and account for most heritable cases and some apparently sporadic ones, but penetrance is low, so a second hit such as an environmental or genetic modifier is thought to be needed. Idiopathic disease is most common in young women.

blocks.title: From BMPR2 loss to cor pulmonale
steps: BMPR2 loss weakens SMAD antiproliferative signaling
Smooth muscle and endothelial cells proliferate
Medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, plexiform lesions
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises
Right ventricle hypertrophies against higher afterload
RV dilates and fails: cor pulmonale
blocks.caption: Remodeling, not just constriction, makes the resistance fixed.

blocks.text: In all groups the pulmonary arteries remodel. Muscular arteries show medial hypertrophy and arterioles become muscularized; the intima develops fibrosis, concentric and laminated (onion skin) in severe disease. Plexiform lesions are characteristic of advanced group 1 disease and long-standing congenital shunts. The large elastic pulmonary arteries develop atherosclerosis, which does not occur at normal pulmonary pressures.

The right ventricle first hypertrophies concentrically, then dilates, and tricuspid regurgitation follows. Cor pulmonale is this right ventricular disease caused by lung or pulmonary vascular disease, excluding left heart and congenital causes. Exertional dyspnea and fatigue reflect a cardiac output that cannot rise; exertional chest pain and syncope reflect right ventricular ischemia and a fixed output. Signs include a loud pulmonic component of S2, a right ventricular heave, and, with failure, raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema. The ECG shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy.

sections.title: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia

blocks.text: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a direct connection between a pulmonary artery and a pulmonary vein through a thin-walled sac with no capillary bed. Most occur in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome), an autosomal dominant disorder of TGF-beta superfamily signaling in endothelium. Mutations in ENG (endoglin) or ACVRL1 (ALK1) account for most cases, and SMAD4 mutations cause a combined juvenile polyposis and HHT syndrome. Abnormal vessel maturation produces fragile, dilated vessels that connect arteries directly to veins.

blocks.title: Vascular lesions in HHT
rows: Recurrent epistaxis, often the first sign
Chronic bleeding and iron deficiency anemia
Hemorrhage; high-output heart failure from large liver shunts
blocks.caption: Small lesions bleed; large lesions shunt.

blocks.text: Blood crossing a pulmonary AVM never meets alveolar gas, so it is a true right-to-left shunt. Mixing shunted blood with oxygenated blood lowers PaO2 and widens the A-a gradient, and because shunted blood never sees the enriched alveolar gas, breathing 100% oxygen raises PaO2 only slightly. PaCO2 stays normal or low, since chemoreceptors increase ventilation and the steep CO2 curve lets normal units compensate. Chronic hypoxemia causes cyanosis, digital clubbing, and secondary polycythemia, and a bruit may be heard over the lesion. Because most AVMs are in the lower lobes, which receive more flow when upright, dyspnea and desaturation can worsen on sitting or standing (platypnea and orthodeoxia).

The pulmonary capillary bed normally filters small venous clots, air, and bacteria. An AVM bypasses this filter, so venous thrombi reach the systemic arteries and cause paradoxical embolic stroke or transient ischemic attack, and bacteria from the mouth or skin seed the brain, causing cerebral abscess. The thin sac can rupture, producing hemoptysis or hemothorax. On a bubble contrast echocardiogram, bubbles appear in the left atrium more than three beats after the right, which places the shunt in the lung, whereas a patent foramen ovale lets bubbles cross within about three beats.

blocks.predict: A patient with a pulmonary AVM and a patient with pneumonia both have PaO2 55 mmHg on room air. Which will show the smaller rise in PaO2 on 100% oxygen, and why?
blocks.explain: The AVM patient. Pneumonia causes partly low V/Q units, whose alveolar PO2 rises with enriched gas. AVM blood bypasses alveoli entirely, so added oxygen reaches only the normal units, whose blood is already nearly saturated and can carry little extra oxygen.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology set the rules. The lung's dual circulation, its low-pressure arteries, and the right ventricle's thin wall explain why emboli usually cause hemorrhage rather than infarction, why sudden obstruction kills through right heart failure, and why chronic pressure overload produces hypertrophy and cor pulmonale. Starling forces and lymphatic drainage explain edema, while V/Q mismatch, dead space, and shunt explain the blood gases: low PaO2 with low PaCO2 in embolism, and hypoxemia that oxygen barely corrects in AVMs.

Pathology links these to other systems. Hematology supplies Virchow triad, D-dimer, and DIC; cardiology supplies left heart failure as the cause of cardiogenic edema, group 2 hypertension, and permissive conditions for infarction; genetics supplies BMPR2, ENG, and ACVRL1, all in TGF-beta signaling; and neurology receives paradoxical emboli and abscesses. The same lab or imaging finding can have several causes: a high D-dimer, a raised wedge pressure, or a wide A-a gradient must be read with the setting, not alone.

summary: Pulmonary edema forms when Starling filtration outpaces lymph flow; cardiogenic edema has a wedge pressure above 18 mmHg and low-protein fluid, noncardiogenic edema a normal wedge pressure.
Chronic pulmonary venous congestion leaves hemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells).
About 95% of pulmonary emboli come from leg DVT, favored by stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.
Embolism causes dead space and low V/Q units, giving hypoxemia, a wide A-a gradient, and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis.
A saddle embolus suddenly raises right ventricular afterload, causing acute dilation, septal shift, low output, and possible sudden death.

Fat embolism appears 24 to 72 hours after long bone fracture with hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae; air embolism follows central lines or rapid ascent; amniotic fluid embolism causes collapse and DIC at delivery.
Pulmonary infarcts are wedge-shaped, red, pleura-based, and mostly lower lobe, occurring when bronchial flow is poor; they cause pleuritic pain and hemoptysis.

Pulmonary hypertension (mean pressure above about 20 mmHg) is grouped as arterial (BMPR2), left heart, lung or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic, or multifactorial; vessels show medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, and plexiform lesions.
HHT is autosomal dominant; pulmonary AVMs are true shunts that cause oxygen-resistant hypoxemia, paradoxical stroke, and brain abscess.

verify: Pulmonary hypertension is defined here as mean pulmonary artery pressure above about 20 mmHg at rest (current international consensus); older sources and many review books use 25 mmHg or more. Confirm the cutoff NABNE expects, and whether the precapillary wedge cutoff of 15 mmHg is tested.
The wedge pressure cutoff of 18 mmHg for cardiogenic edema comes from the older ARDS definition; current ARDS criteria no longer require a wedge pressure. Confirm how NABNE frames it.

Pulmonary Starling values (capillary pressure about 7 mmHg, interstitial pressure about -8 mmHg, interstitial oncotic pressure about 14 mmHg) are Guyton and Hall figures; other texts give different interstitial values, so the worked example is approximate.

Figures for the share of emboli from leg DVT (about 95%), infarction after embolism (about 10%), lower lobe infarcts (about three quarters), and air volume needed for symptoms (over about 100 mL) follow Robbins and vary among sources.
Mortality of amniotic fluid embolism is quoted from about 20% to over 80% depending on era and source, so this chapter says only that it is high.
The proportion of HHT patients with pulmonary AVMs and of pulmonary AVMs due to HHT varies widely among series and is not stated here.
